title: Linux release leg builds on floating `ubuntu-latest`, so the AppImage/.deb require glibc >= 2.38 and cannot start on Ubuntu 22.04 / Debian 12 / RHEL 9 despite 'runs on most distributions'
evidence:
release.yml:105-108
          - os: ubuntu-latest
            rust_target: x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
            recipe: build-linux-updater
            artifact: linux

objdump -T on a workspace binary built on this Ubuntu 24.04 (glibc 2.39) box:
0000000000000000      DF *UND*	0000000000000000 (GLIBC_2.38) __isoc23_sscanf
0000000000000000      DF *UND*	0000000000000000 (GLIBC_2.38) __isoc23_strtol
0000000000000000  w   DF *UND*	0000000000000000 (GLIBC_2.39) pidfd_spawnp

README.md:225-229
- **`azapptoolkit_<version>_amd64.AppImage`** — portable, runs on most
  distributions; `chmod +x` it and run.
- **`azapptoolkit_<version>_amd64.deb`** — for Debian/Ubuntu and
  derivatives

release.yml:301 (release body)
            (Row "artifacts/bundle-linux/appimage/*.AppImage" "Portable, runs on most distros (**auto-updates**); ``chmod +x`` then run."),
rationale: glibc symbol versioning binds each import to the default version of the *build* host's libc, and glibc 2.38 redirected `strtol`/`sscanf` to `__isoc23_*` under `_GNU_SOURCE`. The objdump above shows those as strong (non-weak) imports in a binary from this very workspace built on 2.39; the desktop binary additionally compiles aws-lc-sys C code, so its floor is at least the same. `ubuntu-latest` is 24.04 today (glibc 2.39) and will float again to 26.04, so the artifact's minimum distro silently changes with GitHub's runner image. Ubuntu 22.04 LTS (2.35, supported to 2027), Debian 12 (2.36) and RHEL 9 (2.34) all fail at load with "version `GLIBC_2.38' not found" — the .deb even installs cleanly first. The README/release body promise the opposite, and nothing in release.yml checks the floor. Tauri's own guidance is to build Linux bundles on the oldest distro you intend to support. Note the AppImage bundling WebKitGTK does not help; glibc is never bundled.
proposal: Pin the Linux matrix leg to `ubuntu-22.04` (or the oldest distro the README promises), and add a post-build guard step in the same job: `objdump -T target/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/release/azapptoolkit | grep -oE 'GLIBC_[0-9.]+' | sort -Vu | tail -1` asserted <= 2.35 so a runner-image drift fails the release instead of shipping. Document the actual floor ("needs glibc 2.35+, i.e. Ubuntu 22.04 / Debian 12 or newer") in README Linux install and the release-body Row text, and note that the runner pin is load-bearing in release-updater-demo.md. Consider the same pin for the ci.yml Linux jobs only if they produce shipped bytes (they do not today).
verifier_notes: Reproduced the evidence rather than trusting it: on this Ubuntu 24.04 / glibc 2.39 box, target/debug/deps/azapptoolkit_auth-*, _graph-*, _arm-*, _exchange-*, _keyvault-* all import strong `DF (GLIBC_2.38) __isoc23_sscanf` and `__isoc23_strtol` (pidfd_spawnp/pidfd_getpid are weak, harmless). `nm -u target/debug/build/aws-lc-sys-*/out/libaws_lc_0_45_0_crypto.a` shows both `__isoc23_*` as undefined references, so the floor comes from aws-lc-sys C code compiled with the host gcc; Cargo.lock lists `desktop` (the app crate), rustls, rcgen, quinn-proto and x509-parser as aws-lc-rs dependents and the workspace reqwest is rustls-only (Cargo.toml:29), so the shipped binary inherits it. Control: the pure-Rust target/debug/examples/score_bench tops out at GLIBC_2.34. release.yml:105-108 uses floating `ubuntu-latest`; ci.yml Linux jobs also use it but ship nothing. No glibc/distro floor is documented anywhere (README:225-229 and release.yml:301 promise 'most distros'; docs/architecture/release-updater-demo.md:13 just restates ubuntu-latest; CHANGELOG silent). Tauri's own docs (tauri-docs v2 distribute/appimage.mdx:20) say to build on the oldest base you intend to support and name Ubuntu 22.04 / Debian 12; tauri-action's README example uses ubuntu-22.04. tauri-bundler debian.rs:204-206 writes only the configured Depends (no versioned libc6), so the .deb does install cleanly before failing at launch. Two corrections to the proposal, not the finding: the binary is `desktop` (apps/desktop/src-tauri/Cargo.toml [[bin]] name = "desktop"), so the objdump guard path is `target/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/release/desktop`, not `.../azapptoolkit`; and GitHub retires `ubuntu-22.04` runners around Ubuntu 22.04's April 2027 EOL, so the pin needs a dated note or a container-based build (e.g. debian:bookworm) as the durable form. Severity high is fair for release artifacts that cannot start on Debian stable / the previous Ubuntu LTS while the README says otherwise.
recheck_notes: release.yml:105-108 runs the only shipped-Linux leg (`build-linux-updater` -> `cargo tauri build --target x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu ... --bundles appimage,deb`, justfile:413-414) on floating `ubuntu-latest` (glibc 2.39 on 24.04, and will float higher); no step checks a glibc floor, and `objdump -T` on a workspace test binary built on this glibc 2.39 box shows STRONG (non-weak) `GLIBC_2.38` imports `__isoc23_sscanf` / `__isoc23_strtol` (only the 2.39 `pidfd_*` symbols are weak). Those come from C code linked into the same dependency graph the desktop binary uses (aws-lc-sys and ring are in Cargo.lock), so the release AppImage/.deb inherit at least a 2.38 floor. glibc is never bundled by Tauri's AppImage (linuxdeploy excludelist) and the .deb's generated Depends carries no versioned libc6, so Ubuntu 22.04 (2.35), Debian 12 (2.36) and RHEL 9 (2.34) fail at dynamic-load time with `GLIBC_2.38 not found` after installing cleanly. Docs promise the opposite: README.md:225-229 ('runs on most distributions'), README Requirements ('a modern x86_64 Linux desktop with WebKitGTK'), release.yml:~301 release-body row ('runs on most distros'), and docs/architecture/release-updater-demo.md:13 records `ubuntu-latest` without noting the runner pin is load-bearing. Could not refute: no pin, no guard, no documented floor. Severity kept high because the artifact is a hard startup failure on still-supported LTS distributions that the documentation explicitly claims to cover; if the maintainers consider Linux best-effort (README says Windows is the primary target) this could reasonably be medium, but the fix (pin `ubuntu-22.04` + an objdump floor assertion + a documented floor) is small and the proposal is correct.

title: MSI and .deb installs are offered the NSIS/AppImage payload: no install-format gate in check_for_update although bundle_type() is available
rationale: The plugin resolves the download key as `{os}-{arch}-{bundle}` then `{os}-{arch}`; latest.json only carries the bare keys, so an MSI or .deb install gets `Some(update)` and the shell toasts "Update available" on every launch. On an MSI install, clicking "Update & restart" downloads the NSIS setup.exe, `extract_exe` classifies it as Nsis and `ShellExecuteW(setup.exe /P /UPDATE /R)` installs a second, per-user copy beside the per-machine MSI — exactly the outcome README:255-258 tells MSI users to avoid, and the only documented guard is the opt-out that F036/F139 found is never read. On a .deb install, `bundle_type()` is Deb so `install_deb` runs on AppImage bytes, fails `is_deb` after the full download and the raw plugin string "invalid updater binary format" lands in the splash's warn Callout (update_splash.rs:40-43). The manual "Check for updates" menu item (shell.rs:196-208) has the same blind spot. Tauri exposes the install format at runtime — `tauri::utils::platform::bundle_type()` (tauri re-exports `tauri_utils as utils`, lib.rs:115; the bundler binary-patches the `__TAURI_BUNDLE_TYPE` marker) — and the plugin already relies on it. Complements, does not duplicate, F036/F139.
proposal: In `check_for_update` (and `perform_update`), read `tauri::utils::platform::bundle_type()` and short-circuit for `Some(BundleType::Msi | BundleType::Deb | BundleType::Rpm)`. Preferably make the DTO a tri-state (`UpToDate` / `Available(UpdateInfo)` / `ManagedExternally { format }`) so the manual check can say "This MSI/.deb install is updated by your packaging tooling" instead of "You're on the latest version", and the launch check stays silent. Pull the decision into a pure `fn updatable_format(BundleType) -> bool` with a unit test, mock the new shape in the GUI shell test. Alternative worth weighing: publish `windows-x86_64-msi` and `linux-x86_64-deb` keys in latest.json (the plugin can run msiexec /passive and dpkg via pkexec) and drop the "not auto-updated" policy — but that is a policy change; the gate is the safe default.
verifier_notes: Every quoted line is real and the chain holds end to end. apps/desktop/src-tauri/src/commands/updater.rs:26-37 and :44-49 call `updater.check()` with no install-format gate. Vendored tauri-plugin-updater-2.12.0 src/updater.rs:581-582 derives the installer from `bundle_type()`, `get_urls` (:608-635) falls back from `{os}-{arch}-{installer}` to the bare `{os}-{arch}` key, and release.yml:213-215 publishes only bare keys — so an MSI or .deb install always resolves to the NSIS/AppImage payload. Windows `extract_exe` (:994-1004) classifies the bytes as NSIS regardless of the installed format and `install_inner` (:841-870) ShellExecutes it with `/P /UPDATE`; Linux `install_inner` (:1045-1049) routes a Deb bundle_type to `install_deb` (:1126-1131) which fails `is_deb` on AppImage bytes → `InvalidUpdaterFormat`, after the whole download. Premise that the runtime knows its format is verified against the pinned toolchain: release.yml:138 installs tauri-cli 2.11.5, whose tauri-bundler 2.9.4 `crates/tauri-bundler/src/bundle.rs:36-68` patches `__TAURI_BUNDLE_TYPE_VAR_{DEB,RPM,APP,NSS,MSI}` into the binary, and tauri-utils-2.9.3 platform.rs:353-370 reads it (`tauri::utils` re-export at tauri-2.11.6 lib.rs:115). Frontend: shell.rs:163-176 toasts 'Update available' on every launch for any `Ok(Some)`; the manual check (:183-201) opens the splash. Not a deliberate decision: README.md:236-239 states the MSI and .deb 'are not auto-updated', which the code contradicts; README:255-258 only tells MSI users to use the opt-out that F036/F139 show is never read, and .deb has no documented mitigation at all. Proposal fits repo conventions (pure `updatable_format` fn + unit test; a tri-state DTO means a bindings change, a demo fixture update and a CHANGELOG line since the manual-check message changes). One implementation caveat: `bundle_type()` is `None` for dev builds and raw binaries, so the gate must default to 'updatable' (fall through), never block. Severity high is honest: the enterprise audience is steered to the MSI, then nagged every launch, and one click produces the second conflicting install the README warns about.
recheck_notes: Traced end to end. apps/desktop/src-tauri/src/commands/updater.rs:26-37 and 44-72 call `app.updater().check()` with no install-format gate; tauri.conf.json has no `installer`/`target` override. In the vendored tauri-plugin-updater 2.12.0 (`updater.rs:581-582` + `get_urls` 606-636) the installer comes from `installer_for_bundle_type(bundle_type())` and the lookup order is `{os}-{arch}-{installer}` then bare `{os}-{arch}`; release.yml:213-215 publishes only the bare `windows-x86_64` / `darwin-aarch64` / `linux-x86_64` keys, so an MSI or .deb install always resolves to the NSIS/AppImage payload and `check()` returns `Some(update)` for every newer release. Downstream: Windows `extract_exe` (updater.rs:994-1004) classifies by bytes (`infer::app::is_exe` -> Nsis) regardless of the running bundle type and `install_inner` runs it via ShellExecuteW with `install_mode.nsis_args()` + `/UPDATE` (841-869, 890-913), i.e. an NSIS per-user install beside the per-machine MSI, exactly what README.md:255-258 warns about. Linux `install_inner` (1045-1049) dispatches on `bundle_type()`; for Deb it runs `install_deb` (1126-1131) which fails `infer::archive::is_deb` on AppImage bytes with `InvalidUpdaterFormat` after the full download, surfaced verbatim via `updater_err` into the splash's `error` signal (update_splash.rs ~40-43). The runtime signal exists: tauri-utils 2.9.3 `platform::bundle_type()` (platform.rs:344-368) reads the `__TAURI_BUNDLE_TYPE` marker that tauri-cli 2.11.5 (pinned in release.yml:138 / scripts/setup.sh:57) binary-patches per bundle, and `tauri` 2.11.6 re-exports `tauri_utils as utils`, so the proposed gate is implementable as a safe call. Frontend confirms both surfaces: shell.rs:167-176 toasts on every launch when `Some(info)`, and the manual check at 189-200 reports 'You're on the latest version' only on `None`. The documented mitigation (`auto_update` opt-out) is defined in crates/azapptoolkit-core/src/settings.rs but no consumer exists in apps/desktop/src-tauri/src or web-rs/src (grep for `auto_update`/`UserSettings::load` returns nothing outside core), so MSI deployments have no working guard. Severity kept high: MSI is the documented enterprise rollout path (release body line ~296) and the harmful path is one click away from a toast shown on every launch; the .deb leg degrades to a raw plugin error rather than data loss, which alone would be medium.

title: macOS: unsigned .app + legacy-keychain default ACL means every auto-update triggers a keychain prompt (or a silent 'no session') — README says it 'updates in place like the Windows NSIS build'
evidence:
README.md:217-219
After that it launches normally and **updates in place** like the Windows
NSIS build. Apple Silicon (M-series) only for now; Intel builds aren't
published yet.

token_cache.rs:55-57 (legacy keychain store, default ACL)
        let store =
            apple_native_keyring_store::keychain::Store::new().map_err(|e| e.to_string())?;

vendored apple-native-keyring-store/src/keychain.rs:72-74
        self.get_keychain()?
            .set_generic_password(&self.service, &self.account, secret)

DEVELOPMENT.md:161-164
The builds are **unsigned / not notarized**, so first launch hits
Gatekeeper — ...  (Apple notarization
can be layered on later by adding the Developer-ID secrets + `APPLE_*` env

commands/auth.rs:39-43 (a keyring error at launch is swallowed)
        Err(err) => {
            let code = UiError::from(err).code;
            tracing::info!(target: "auth", %code, "no session to restore; showing sign-in");
            Ok(None)
rationale: Legacy-keychain items created with `SecKeychainAddGenericPassword` get an ACL naming the creating application. For code without a Developer-ID signature there is no stable designated requirement — the trusted-app entry is bound to the specific binary — so after the updater swaps `/Applications/azapptoolkit.app` (plugin `install_inner`, rename of the bundle) the new binary is a different app to Keychain Services. The next `find_generic_password` in `restore_session` raises the system "azapptoolkit wants to use your confidential information stored in 'azapptoolkit'" dialog; "Always Allow" only lasts until the next update, and "Deny" surfaces as `AuthError::Keyring`, which `restore_session` turns into `Ok(None)` — the operator lands on the sign-in card with no hint that the update caused it, and the subsequent sign-in's `set_generic_password` on the existing item can hit the same ACL again and fail with the misleading `keyring` hint "unlock your keychain". None of this is written down: README/DEVELOPMENT.md cover only the one-time Gatekeeper bypass. Reasoned from Apple's keychain ACL model and the vendored store code; not observed on hardware (no macOS here).
proposal: Short term (docs, S): add to README's macOS section and the Updates section that, because the build is unsigned, macOS asks for keychain access again after every update — choose **Always Allow**; and that a post-update launch that lands on the sign-in card is this, not a revoked session. Medium term: treat Developer-ID signing (stable `identifier + team` designated requirement) as the fix rather than only notarization, and say so in the DEVELOPMENT.md macOS paragraph. Optionally, on macOS only, have `restore_session` log the `keyring` code at warn when the stored version in settings.json differs from CARGO_PKG_VERSION, so support can recognise it.
verifier_notes: Quoted evidence is real: README.md:217-219 ('updates in place like the Windows NSIS build'); crates/azapptoolkit-auth/src/token_cache.rs:52-57 registers `apple_native_keyring_store::keychain::Store` (the crate's legacy-keychain store; its `protected` module is the data-protection keychain, which needs a signed, entitled app and so is not an option here); vendored apple-native-keyring-store-1.0.2 src/keychain.rs:72-74/79-82 use `set_generic_password` / `find_generic_password` (SecKeychain* items with per-item ACLs); docs/DEVELOPMENT.md:161-164 says unsigned / not notarized; apps/desktop/src-tauri/src/commands/auth.rs:37-43 turns every restore error into `Ok(None)` with only an info-level code; dto/lib.rs:168 maps `AuthError::Keyring` → `keyring`, and token_cache.rs:297/352/392 wrap every store error into it. Nothing in README, docs/ or CHANGELOG mentions a keychain prompt (README:326 only says tokens live in Keychain). The mechanism — a legacy-keychain ACL trusted-application entry bound to an unsigned/ad-hoc-signed binary's identity, invalidated when the updater swaps the .app — is standard macOS behaviour (the well-known post-update 'wants to use your confidential information' prompt for unsigned apps), and the reviewer is upfront that it is reasoned rather than observed. Category docs / severity medium is honest: cheap fix, and without it a post-update launch that silently lands on the sign-in card looks like a revoked session. The optional 'log at warn when the stored version differs' item overlaps the startup-diagnostics cluster (F477/F484) and should be deduplicated there.

title: audit.rs tests the cache guard exhaustively but nothing tests what feeds `degraded`; score_one's swallowed SP lookup (F023) returns a clean Ok(AuditItem) the guard cannot see
rationale: The predicate test proves 'degraded non-empty blocks the cache' for all 8 combinations, and `a_dead_session_stops_the_audit_but_one_bad_app_does_not` (1621) proves whole-item failures classify correctly — but a failed SP lookup becomes neither: score_one returns `Ok(AuditItem)` with `orgwide == HashSet::new()`, so the run scores the app as scoped, `degraded` stays empty and the guard is fed a lie. `ScoreCtx` (860-880) is `Arc<GraphClient>` + `Arc<Cache>` + resolver, i.e. constructible over wiremock, so this is a missing producer test, not an untestable path.
proposal: Make score_one report coverage: return `(AuditItem, Option<AuditCoverageGap>)` or take `&Mutex<Vec<AuditCoverageGap>>`, pushing `GraphAppRoleAssignments` (or a new `ServicePrincipalLookup`) on the Err arm. Add `a_failed_sp_lookup_degrades_the_run_and_blocks_the_cache`: wiremock `GET /v1.0/servicePrincipals?$filter=appId eq 'app-1'` -> 503 (retry budget exhausted), one app with a Graph mail role granted; assert the gap is reported and `run_is_cacheable(false, false, &degraded) == false`. F029's source-scan pin of the `cache.put` guard is complementary, not a substitute.
verifier_notes: Verified: `score_one` swallows the lean SP lookup error to `None` and returns `Ok(AuditItem)` (audit.rs:1490-1497); the only `degraded` producers are the three tenant-wide gaps (246), `PerPrincipalScoring` (381) and `PermissionResolution` (389) — none inside `score_one`. The exhaustive guard test (1664-1680) tests only the predicate. Reachability nuance worth recording: `seed_lean_sps_from_index` (graph service_principals.rs:284-314) seeds only positive matches and is capped at the bucket size, so an app not in the index (or beyond the cap) falls to a live `GET /servicePrincipals?$filter=appId eq` in `get_service_principal_by_app_id_lean` (91-98) that can fail independently of the already-gapped index read — so the swallowed Err is a real, uncovered hole with a healthy index. With `sp == None` the app loses `has_admin_consent` and its org-wide grant lookup and is scored as holding nothing, and `run_is_cacheable` is fed an empty `degraded`. `ScoreCtx` (860-880) is plain Arcs/maps so a wiremock producer test is feasible. `ServicePrincipalIndex` gap (1170) covers the whole-index failure only. Medium is fair.

title: audit_cancel is shared by the read-only audit, every bulk write and the AAP migration, and the UI can run them concurrently, so any Cancel button stops all of them
rationale: Generation arithmetic: audit claims (current=1, token g=1), then a bulk scope-and-strip/delete claims (current=2, g=2). Pressing Cancel in EITHER the posture strip (cancel_audit) or the BulkProgressRow (cancel_bulk) runs cancel(): cancelled = max(0, 2) = 2, and both 2>=1 and 2>=2 hold, so both runs stop. The reverse start order gives the same result. There is no ordering in which cross-kind collateral cancellation does not happen. Consequences: (1) the operator cancels a read-only scan and a tenant WRITE (bulk delete, scope mailbox/SharePoint access, add owner, disable sign-in, AAP migration) halts mid-selection, reporting 'N app(s) were never attempted' for a Cancel they never pressed on it; (2) the operator cancels a bulk run and the audit result comes back cancelled=true, uncached, and the Security strip shows 'This scan was cancelled early — X of Y principals were scored' (security_view.rs:236-246) — a coverage caveat for a cancel that never targeted the scan. The CancelFlag::cancel doc justifies stopping older generations as 'a run that was going to be superseded anyway', which only holds when all runs on a flag are the same kind; the docstrings' 'never run at once' premise is false given keep-alive views and per-component busy signals, so this is not a documented trade-off. The same overlap also means every mounted BulkActionBar's `use_progress_stream(progress, events::bulk_progress)` (bulk_action_bar.rs:391-392) receives BOTH producers' events, so two concurrent bulk rows show interleaved done/total.
proposal: Give each run kind its own identity. Minimal (S): add `bulk_cancel: CancelFlag` and `migration_cancel: CancelFlag` to AppState, point `cancel_bulk` and all `bulk_*` claims at `bulk_cancel`, the AAP migration at its own flag, and pin the command->flag mapping in repo_invariants/cancel.rs (e.g. a `bulk_*` command body must claim `bulk_cancel`, `run_audit` must claim `audit_cancel`). Robust (M): have `claim()` return the generation to the command, emit it in the first progress event (`run_id` on BulkProgress/AuditProgress), and add a `cancel_run(run_id)` command that does `cancelled.fetch_max(run_id)` only when it is the current generation — then each Cancel button stops exactly its own run and progress listeners can filter by run_id, fixing the interleaved bulk-progress rows too. Update the docstrings at bulk.rs:127, bulk.rs:143-145, audit.rs:14 and caching-and-search.md:350 to state the real rule.
verifier_notes: Evidence is real. bulk.rs:125-134 asserts the audit and bulk loops 'never run at once'; that premise is false: views are keep-alive (web-rs/src/lib.rs:274,288 via util.rs:24-52 display toggle), BulkActionBar gates only on its own `busy` (bulk_action_bar.rs:459-461,620), AuditController::run gates only on `scanning` and never clears `result` (controller.rs:182-207), and AuditAppsPane renders its BulkActionBar whenever `total_items` is Some (audit_view/mod.rs:226-247) — so a re-scan leaves the table + bar usable. BulkActionBar is also hosted in application_list.rs:563, findings.rs:371, sso_certificates_dashboard.rs:108 and bulk_actions_view.rs:226, all reachable during a scan. All 10 bulk commands (bulk.rs:156,319,418,541,616,674,724,774,842,905) and the AAP migration (aap_migration.rs:52) claim audit_cancel; cancel() at state.rs:94-97 stamps `current`, so either Cancel stops every generation on the flag. Not a documented trade-off: the repo's own intent is that unrelated runs must not cross-cancel (state.rs:218-227 field docs, backup.rs:62-63, sharepoint.rs:823-825, and the `distinct_cancel_flags_are_independent` test at state.rs:733-744); the CancelFlag::cancel 'superseded anyway' rationale (state.rs:90-93) only holds for same-kind runs. caching-and-search.md:350 restates the sharing without the concurrency premise. Severity lowered from high to medium: no data corruption or leak — a bulk run stops at an item boundary and names the unattempted remainder (CHANGELOG 'A stopped bulk run no longer hides the apps it never reached'), the audit result is flagged cancelled and never cached (audit.rs:441-446), and both are re-runnable; the harm is a wrong-target cancel plus a misleading coverage caveat. title: GraphClient has a single throttle_observer slot, so concurrent fan-outs on one tenant overwrite each other's tracker and ThrottleGuard::drop clears whichever run's observer is installed
rationale: Each FanOutMeter::attach does build its own ConcurrencyThrottle (no shared tracker), and the recovery loop terminates within one 30 s tick after the last Arc drops (Weak upgrade fails -> break), so those two parts are sound. But the observer slot is one `Option` per GraphClient, and the audit, bulk delete/grant/expired-sweep, site sweep and DR backup all run against the same `Arc<GraphClient>` for the tenant. When run B attaches while run A is in flight, A's tracker is silently replaced: A's 429s now halve B's cap and A's own cap never halves again. When either guard drops first, `clear_throttle_observer()` removes the OTHER run's observer for the rest of its life, so a still-running fan-out runs with a fixed cap and no back-off — exactly the 'stale/missing observer' failure the guard exists to prevent, now in the concurrent case the guard's doc never considers. Distinct from F020 (halving window) and F031 (tick ordering).
proposal: Make the slot multi-observer: `RwLock<Vec<Weak<dyn ThrottleObserver>>>`, `set_throttle_observer` pushes, `on_throttle` notifies every live Weak and prunes dead ones, and `ThrottleGuard::drop` removes only its own tracker (`Weak::ptr_eq`). Alternatively keep the single slot but make `clear_throttle_observer` a compare-and-clear (`Arc::ptr_eq` against the guard's own tracker) and log when an attach displaces a live observer. Add a unit test in client/tests/transport.rs that attaches two observers and asserts both see a 429 and that dropping one guard leaves the other attached.
verifier_notes: Evidence real: client.rs:143 is a single `RwLock<Option<Arc<dyn ThrottleObserver>>>`, set_throttle_observer overwrites and clear_throttle_observer unconditionally clears (client.rs:262-268); ThrottleGuard::drop calls clear (throttle.rs:140-144). All attach sites use the shared per-tenant Arc from graph_for (audit.rs:133, bulk.rs:185 etc., sharepoint.rs:864 via sharepoint_client_checked:129, backup.rs:88), and concurrent fan-outs on one tenant are the normal case given keep-alive views (see finding 0). The only test (client/tests/transport.rs:267-297 `throttle_observer_fires_on_429`) attaches one observer; nothing in repo_invariants/fanout.rs pins observer lifetime. transport.rs:557 snapshots the observer per request, so an in-flight request notifies whichever tracker was installed when it started — consistent with the finding. Consequence is degraded adaptive back-off, not correctness: the transport still retries 429s honouring Retry-After (transport.rs:626-631), so the surviving run finishes at a fixed cap — the pre-adaptive behaviour sharepoint.rs:858-862 describes as the problem the throttle was added to fix. Medium is defensible given the repo built a RAII guard specifically to prevent a milder stale-observer case; the compare-and-clear (`Arc::ptr_eq`) variant is the smaller correct fix and the multi-observer Vec<Weak> the complete one.

title: Startup panics with zero diagnostics if the log file cannot be created: install_tracing `.expect()`s the appender before any subscriber or panic hook exists
rationale: `create_dir_all`'s error is ignored, then `build()` is unwrapped. On a read-only or unwritable app-data dir (locked-down %APPDATA% redirection, a sandboxed/kiosk profile, HOME unset so the fallback is the install directory) the very first thing the process does is panic — before `install_panic_hook` and before any `tracing` subscriber — so a double-clicked GUI app 'just doesn't open', the advertised log directory holds nothing, and stderr is invisible. The panic hook's own doc comment (lib.rs:374-378) explains exactly why an unlogged crash is unacceptable; this path defeats it.
proposal: Install the panic hook first (it only needs `tracing` macros, which are no-ops until a subscriber exists — or buffer: install a stderr-only subscriber first). Make the file appender optional: `match builder.build(&log_dir) { Ok(a) => Some(non_blocking(a)), Err(e) => { eprintln!(...); None } }`, register the file layer via `.with(file_layer_option)` (tracing-subscriber supports `Option<Layer>`), then after init `tracing::warn!(log_dir = %log_dir.display(), error = %e, "file logging disabled")`. Consider surfacing the same fact in the config screen / About so the operator learns the log is not being written. Effort S.
verifier_notes: Evidence is real: lib.rs:11-12 calls `install_tracing()` before `install_panic_hook()`; lib.rs:340 discards the `create_dir_all` error and lib.rs:353 `.expect("failed to initialize rolling log file appender")`; config_directory() falls back to `PathBuf::from(".")` when APPDATA/HOME is unset (lib.rs:418). tracing-appender 0.2.5 (Cargo.lock) `Builder::build` → `from_builder` → `create_writer` returns `InitError` 'failed to create log directory' / 'failed to create log file' (vendored rolling.rs:189,788-799), so an unwritable app-data dir (or CWD = install dir when APPDATA is unset) panics before any subscriber or hook exists — the process exits with nothing on disk and stderr invisible for a double-clicked app, exactly the failure the panic-hook doc comment (lib.rs:374-378) says is unacceptable. No test or doc treats this as deliberate. The proposal (optional file layer via `.with(Option<Layer>)`, eprintln + post-init warn) is sound; installing the hook first alone would not help (no subscriber yet), so the appender-optional change is the load-bearing part. Likelihood is low but impact is total; medium is defensible.

title: Webview panics and surfaced IPC errors are never persisted to the backend log — no frontend→backend log command exists
rationale: F425 documents that any non-UiError IPC rejection panics the whole WASM app. When that (or any other frontend panic — an `expect` in a view, a Leptos runtime error) happens in a release build, the operator sees a frozen or blank window; the panic message exists only in a devtools console that release builds cannot open, so a bug report can contain nothing but 'it went blank'. The backend log, the one artifact support asks for, is silent because nothing bridges the two worlds.
proposal: Add `#[tauri::command] fn log_frontend(level: String, message: String)` (command + `generate_handler!` + `bindings/diagnostics.rs` stub; cap message length; re-emit at `tracing::{warn,error}!(target: "webview", %message)`). In `run()` set a custom hook that (a) calls `console_error_panic_hook::hook(info)` and (b) SYNCHRONOUSLY calls the JS `invoke` (a `#[wasm_bindgen] extern` to `window.__TAURI_INTERNALS__.invoke` returning a Promise that is dropped — the IPC post happens on the call, not on await) — no `spawn_local` inside the hook. Guard with `is_tauri()` / `not(feature = "demo")` and register a no-op fixture in `demo::register_fixtures` (demo_fixture_coverage.rs). Separately, have `Session::report_command_error_for`'s plain-toast branch call the async binding with `code` + message. Effort M.
verifier_notes: Premise verified: apps/desktop/web-rs/src/lib.rs:69 installs only `console_error_panic_hook::set_once()`; src-tauri/Cargo.toml:32-33 has just updater + dialog plugins (no tauri-plugin-log); tauri.conf.json has no `devtools`; no console/log bridge anywhere in web-rs/src (only the hook dep); README Logs (422-431) covers the backend file only. The F425 premise is also real: tauri-sys (git rev 289bd29, src/core.rs:26) does `swb::from_value(err).unwrap()` on a rejection, so a non-UiError rejection panics the WASM app. However the proposed mechanism will not work: wasm32-unknown-unknown is panic=abort, so after the hook returns the module traps; a `leptos::task::spawn_local` scheduled inside the hook is a microtask that re-enters wasm after the trap, when the instance is in an undefined state — the future is not reliably polled and the IPC never leaves. The hook must issue the IPC synchronously.

title: `unauthorized` (client 401, including the CAE "re-auth needed" path) renders as bare "unauthorized (401)" with no action; the three ui_hints tell the operator to sign out, contradicting the in-place recovery design

Sign in again" (graph_err.rs:88-91) with no control to do so. F353/F427 cover the *dead-session* codes not reaching the sink; this is the 401 class, which reaches the sink and is still a dead end.

Do NOT add the code to `REAUTH_FATAL_CODES`. 3) Reword the three `Unauthorized` ui_hints and `premium_feature_err`'s Unauthorized arm to "use Refresh token (next to Sign out), then retry" — the Exchange `Forbidden { had_diagnostics: false }` hint already uses exactly that phrasing. 4) Add a GUI test next to tests/gui/reauth.rs asserting an `unauthorized` mock produces a toast with a "Refresh token" action.

title: Offline at launch shows the plain sign-in card: `restore_session` folds a `network` failure into `Ok(None)` and the silent restore cannot be retried without relaunching
rationale: The documented rationale ("the card is the recovery, and it already says what to do") holds for the cases the comment lists — nothing stored, a revoked token, a locked keyring — where the correct next step really is to sign in. It does not hold for the case the comment omits: the token endpoint is unreachable (laptop off-network, captive portal, proxy down). The refresh token is still valid (only `InvalidGrant` purges it), yet the operator is told to "Sign in to your tenant"; clicking opens a browser that cannot load login.microsoftonline.com, the loopback listener then waits up to 300 s (F113) and returns `loopback`, whose hint is the generic fallback. Nothing on screen ever says "you appear to be offline", and there is no way to retry the silent restore once connectivity returns short of restarting the app. The backend already computes the code (`UiError::from(err).code`) and throws it away.
proposal: Keep `Result<Option<TenantContext>, UiError>` and, in `restore_session`, return `Err(ui)` only when `ui.code == "network"` (everything else stays `Ok(None)` per the documented rationale, which should be extended to name the offline case). In `Root`, on that `Err` render `SignInScreen` with a warn `Callout` ("Couldn't reach Entra ID to restore your session — check your network connection.") and a "Retry" button that re-invokes `restore_session`; add a GUI test mocking `restore_session` with a `network` error asserting the callout appears and `sign_in` is not called.
verifier_notes: Code is as quoted: apps/desktop/src-tauri/src/commands/auth.rs:37-44 folds every `Err` (including `AuthError::Http` → code `network`) into `Ok(None)` after logging the code; web-rs lib.rs:167-174 ignores errors by design; only `InvalidGrant` purges the refresh token (auth/service/mod.rs:529-540), and `restore_session` (service/mod.rs:603-628) is a live token POST; the interactive loopback waits up to 300 s (service/mod.rs:274). But this is a documented deliberate decision, not an omission: the command's own doc (auth.rs:20-30) states "`Ok(None)` — never an error — is the answer for every way this can come up empty … an error toast at launch would add noise", and only its enumerated cases leave out the offline one. The consequence is also milder than described: the auth HTTP client has a 30 s timeout (service/mod.rs:95) so the restore fails fast; the interactive path ends in `loopback`/`network`, whose sign-in hints (sign_in.rs:155 and the 166 fallback) already say to check the network and retry; and nothing is lost — the keyring token survives and a normal sign-in works once online. The proposal's `RestoreOutcome` enum is a wire-shape change touching the binding, `demo::register_fixtures` and the Root match for a small UX gain.

title: sign_out prunes only graph_clients and exchange_clients; kv_clients, arm_clients and la_clients are never removed anywhere
rationale: Not a credential leak: every client holds a ScopedTokenAdapter that asks the singleton auth service per request (token_adapter.rs:70-80), so a stale client fails with `not_signed_in` after sign-out. But the asymmetry is unexplained, the kv map is keyed per (tenant, vault) and only grows across a long session with several tenants/vaults, and a long-running fan-out that outlives sign-out keeps its `Arc<GraphClient>` and stops only when its next `bearer()` fails (dispatch::SessionDead) — sign_out cancels none of the three flags, so a bulk write continues until that failure and a run in its final local phase can still `cache.put` a `{tenant}|…` entry (e.g. audit.rs:441-446) after `invalidate_tenant` swept the tenant. The window is small, but it is the same-tenant/different-operator case the sign_out comment says it exists to prevent.
proposal: In sign_out remove the tenant's entries from all five client maps (`kv_clients.lock().retain(|(t, _), _| t != &tenant.tenant_id)` plus arm/la `remove`), and add a repo_invariants check that every `Mutex<HashMap<…>>` client field on AppState is referenced in sign_out (or document why graph/exchange are the only two). Drop the 'cancel all three flags on sign_out' part, or tenant-scope it: the flags are process-wide, so cancelling them on sign-out of tenant A would also abort a run on tenant B, and in-flight runs already stop at their next `bearer()` via the SessionDead latch. The post-invalidate `cache.put` window is real but tiny and tenant-scoped; if it matters, guard the final put on the session still being signed in rather than on a flag.
verifier_notes: Asymmetry confirmed: auth.rs:54-55 prunes only graph_clients and exchange_clients, while state.rs:207-214 declares kv_clients/arm_clients/la_clients, which are referenced nowhere outside state.rs (never pruned, kv keyed per (tenant, vault) so it grows monotonically). Introduced with the sign_out clearing in 06af5cc with no comment on why only two maps. Not a credential leak — every client holds a ScopedTokenAdapter that asks the auth singleton per request (token_adapter.rs:70-80). The cancel-flags proposal is the weak part: CancelFlag instances are process-wide, not per tenant, so the proposed `audit_cancel.cancel()` etc. in a per-tenant sign_out has cross-tenant side effects, and the runs it would stop already terminate via dispatch::SessionDead on the next token failure. The cache.put-after-invalidate observation (audit.rs:441-446) is accurate but the window is a few local statements and the data is the same tenant's.

title: Credential-expiry roll-up is stored with plain `put` although the `put_index` doc names it as a pinned tenant-wide index

Use only for tenant-wide *index* entries that cost a full directory scan to rebuild and that several surfaces read — the service-principal index, the app-registration pairing rows, the credential-expiry roll-up. title: Daily debug-level logs (14 files) are written to Roaming AppData on Windows instead of LOCALAPPDATA
rationale: `%APPDATA%` is the Roaming hive; Windows convention (and Tauri's own `PathResolver::app_log_dir`, which resolves to `%LOCALAPPDATA%\<identifier>\logs`) puts logs and caches under Local because Roaming is synchronised with roaming user profiles / FSLogix / UE-V at logon and logoff. The MSI is explicitly marketed for SCCM/Intune/GPO estates — the population most likely to roam profiles — and this app writes at `debug` level for its own crates, two weeks of it, so the profile carries megabytes of request logs (with tenant/object GUIDs) between machines and slows logon. settings.json belongs in Roaming (it is per-user config); the logs do not. The comment at lib.rs:333-337 documents the path but gives no roaming rationale, so this is a convention slip rather than a decision.
proposal: Introduce `log_directory()` per platform: Windows `%LOCALAPPDATA%\azapptoolkit\logs` (fallback to `%APPDATA%` only if LOCALAPPDATA is unset), macOS `~/Library/Logs/azapptoolkit` (the platform convention), Linux `$XDG_STATE_HOME`/`~/.local/state/azapptoolkit/logs` or keep `.local/share` but honour `$XDG_DATA_HOME`. Keep settings.json where it is. Update README Logs + the lib.rs comment, and add a one-line CHANGELOG note since the documented log location changes for operators. Consider a one-time best-effort move of existing log files so support instructions stay valid.

title: A mid-session token-refresh network failure surfaces as non-retryable `token_error`, not `network_error`: `token_adapter::token_error` flattens `AuthError::Http`
rationale: Extends F110 (which covers `consent_required`). The same outage produces two different classifications depending on where it strikes: during the Graph call it is `network_error` (retryable: true, "network: …"); during the lazy refresh that precedes the call (`provider.bearer()` at transport.rs:498, ~every hour) it is `token_error` (retryable: false) with message `token: http: error sending request for url (https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant>/oauth2/v2.0/token)`. The auth-plane spelling `network` is hinted only on the sign-in card, so mid-session it never receives a hint either. Operators and any future `network_error`-specific UI treatment (finding 3) will miss the refresh-time half of network failures.
proposal: In `token_adapter::token_error`, map `AuthError::Http(_)` → "network_error" only; leave `TokenExchange` as `token_error` unless `post_token` is first changed to distinguish 5xx from 4xx. Add a `core::reauth::TRANSIENT_PASSTHROUGH: &[&str] = &["network_error"]` (or extend `passthrough_code` to consult both slices) so the macro's `Token(t)` arm and ExchangeError::ui_code pass it through and `is_retryable` sees it. Pin adapter ↔ dto agreement in the dto agreement tests (lib.rs:254-297): `Http` yields `network` on the auth plane and `network_error` on the client plane, and both are retryable.
verifier_notes: The split is real: token_adapter.rs:21-28 maps every AuthError other than NotSignedIn/RefreshTokenMissing/InvalidGrant/ConsentRequired — so `AuthError::Http` too — to `token_error`; the macro's `Token` arm passes through only `REAUTH_FATAL_CODES` (http_error.rs:131-133, reauth.rs:50-52); `is_retryable_code` excludes `token_error` (http_retry.rs:25-27); `From<AuthError>` maps `Http` → ("network", true) (dto lib.rs:169); the `network` hint exists only on the sign-in card (sign_in.rs:155). So an outage hitting the lazy refresh at graph transport.rs:498 surfaces as non-retryable `token_error` with "token: http: error sending request for url (…)", whereas the same outage one line later is retryable `network_error`. The proposal's second half is wrong, though: `post_token` (auth/service/mod.rs:168-198) returns `TokenExchange(format!("HTTP {status}"))` for EVERY non-2xx the body classifier does not recognise — including 400s for wrong tenant / unknown client — so mapping `TokenExchange` to `server_error` would make permanent failures retryable. The `TRANSIENT_PASSTHROUGH` slice idea is consistent with the existing `passthrough_code` pattern.

title: trunk build --release ships unminified CSS and JS: Trunk's `minify` defaults to `never` and nothing enables it
evidence:
Trunk.toml:1-6: `[build]\ntarget = "index.html"\ndist = "dist"\n# Optimization is selected by the caller's `--release` flag ... so there is no `release` default to set here.` (no `minify` key)
justfile:51-52: `web-build-release:\n    trunk build --release --locked`
index.html:19-22: `data-wasm-opt="z"` ... `<link data-trunk rel="css" href="styles.css" />`

proposal: Add `minify = "on_release"` under `[build]` in apps/desktop/web-rs/Trunk.toml (or `--minify` in `web-build-release` and `web-build-pages`), rebuild once and eyeball the Pages demo for any CSS the minifier changes semantically (custom properties and `@media` blocks are safe). Pin the Trunk version CI installs (`tool: just,trunk` is unpinned in ci.yml/release.yml/pages.yml) so the minifier behaviour is reproducible.
verifier_notes: Trunk.toml:1-6 has no `minify` key and the comment only covers `--release`; justfile:51-52 runs `trunk build --release --locked` (the tauri.conf.json:8 `beforeBuildCommand`) and web-build-pages likewise; styles.css is 120,706 bytes (`wc -c`). Upstream trunk `src/config/models/build.rs` has `/// Control minification. #[serde(default)] pub minify: Minify` and `src/config/types/minify.rs` defines `Minify { #[default] Never, OnRelease, Always }` with `#[serde(rename_all = "snake_case")]`, so `minify = "on_release"` under `[build]` is the correct spelling and the default really is no minification. Minification touches HTML/CSS/JS only; the wasm is already wasm-opt'd (`data-wasm-opt="z"`, index.html:19-22). Modest win, one-line fix, severity low is honest.

title: `UiError.retryable` drives a Retry action at only one toast site; `run_toast_err` discards the op it already holds
rationale: The DTO contract says `retryable` advises a retry button, every client computes it via `is_retryable_code` (throttled/server_error/network_error), and the toast primitive supports a sticky Retry action — yet the only consumer is the admin-consent button in permissions_tab. `report_command_error_for` always passes `None`, and the pinning test (state/mod.rs:722-731) asserts a `network` error with `retryable: true` gets no action. errors.rs:70-74 explains the sink cannot replay because it receives only the `UiError`, but `CommandState::run_toast_err` *does* hold `op`; it just types it `FnOnce` so it cannot be re-invoked. Net effect: a 429/5xx/network failure on any of the ~24 `run`/`run_toast_err` call sites and the ~56 inline `error.set(Some(e.message))` sites is a 10-second auto-dismissing red toast (errors without an action are not sticky, toast.rs:129) with no way back except finding and re-clicking the control — the exact "dead end" the module docs say the sink exists to prevent.
proposal: Scope the change to `CommandState::run_toast_err`: take `op: impl Fn(String) -> Fut + Clone + 'static` there only (leave `run`/`run_with` as FnOnce), and when `e.retryable` build a `ToastAction` that re-invokes `run_toast_err` with the same `on_ok`/`op`, passed through a new `Session::report_command_error_with_retry(&e, feature, Some(retry))`; keep `report_command_error(_for)` behaviour and flip the state/mod.rs:722 pin only for the new entry point. Alternatively trim the "retry button" sentence at crates/azapptoolkit-dto/src/lib.rs:42-43 so the flag's contract matches the one hand-rolled consumer.
verifier_notes: Facts check out: the only `.retryable` consumer is apps/desktop/web-rs/src/views/tabs/permissions_tab.rs:121; `report_command_error_for` always passes `None` (state/errors.rs:160); the pin at state/mod.rs:722-731 asserts a retryable `network` error gets no action; only error toasts WITH an action are sticky (toast.rs `sticky = Error && has_action`); `use_command` takes `op: impl FnOnce` (use_command.rs:49). But the finding overstates the gap: (a) every load-failure surface goes through `DetailLoadError`, which ALWAYS offers Retry regardless of the flag (detail_load_error.rs:6-9), so ignoring `retryable` there is by design; (b) errors.rs:70-74 documents as a decision that the sink receives only the UiError and that call sites holding a re-runnable op replay it themselves; (c) `CommandState::run` puts the message inline next to the control that triggered it, so re-clicking is the retry; (d) counts are approximate — 24 `run`, 16 `run_toast_err` (13 in sso_tab.rs), 9 direct `report_command_error` callers, ~55 `error.set(Some(e.message))`. What is real and worth fixing: the 16 `run_toast_err` sites and 9 direct `report_command_error` sites give a 10 s auto-dismissing toast for a 429/5xx/network failure although `run_toast_err` holds the op. Converting `run`/`run_with` from FnOnce to Fn+Clone across all sites is a larger refactor than the payoff warrants.

title: Backup and restore share dr_cancel and are gated by independent signals in the same view, so cancelling a read-only backup aborts an in-flight restore mid-pass
rationale: The DR view renders the Back up and Restore controls side by side; 'Back up this tenant' is disabled only while `busy` (dr.rs:237) and 'Restore into this tenant…' only while `restoring` (dr.rs:361-366), so an operator can start a backup and, while it walks a large tenant, load a file and start a restore. Both claim dr_cancel (gen 1 and gen 2); cancel_dr stamps current=2, so the backup's Cancel button stops the restore between passes. The restore report then reads '(cancelled before completing — partial)' (dr.rs:494) for a run whose Cancel button was never pressed, leaving shells created without permissions/owners/secrets. The backup-and-restore.md rationale only argues dr_cancel vs audit_cancel; it never considers backup vs restore overlap.
proposal: Frontend S: disable the Restore controls while `busy` and the Back-up button while `restoring` so the two are mutually exclusive on the page. Backend S: add `restore_cancel: CancelFlag` with a `cancel_restore` command so the restore's Cancel is the only thing that can stop a write; keep `cancel_dr` for the backup.
verifier_notes: Evidence real: run_backup gates on `busy` (dr.rs:54-61), do_restore never checks `busy` (dr.rs:150-155), both Cancel handlers call cancel_dr (dr.rs:96-98, 180-182 → backup.rs:331-333), backup_tenant and restore_tenant both claim dr_cancel (backup.rs:78, restore.rs:193); the Back-up button is disabled only by `busy` (dr.rs:237) and Load/Restore only by `restoring` (dr.rs:361-366). The consequence is accurate to the code: restore.rs:240-250 now breaks passes 2-5 on cancel too ('Both stop conditions, in every pass'), so a cancel during pass 1/2 does leave unwired shells — note backup-and-restore.md:173-175 ('never bare shells') is stale relative to that code, and the deep-dive (:126-129) argues only dr_cancel vs audit_cancel, never backup vs restore. Severity lowered to low: triggering it requires backing up a tenant and, mid-run, loading a file and confirming a restore into the same tenant — an unusual sequence — and the report flags the run cancelled. The frontend mutual-exclusion fix (disable Restore while `busy`, Back up while `restoring`) is trivial and sufficient; a separate restore_cancel is optional.

title: `target = "azapptoolkit::graph"` / `"azapptoolkit::cache"` are recorded as a field named `target`, not as the event target, while both layers hide the real target with `with_target(false)`
evidence:
service_principals.rs:188-192:
  tracing::debug!(
      target = "azapptoolkit::graph",
      first_page = page.items.len(),
      "service-principal index first page"
  );
Same form at service_principals.rs:209,216,257; commands/applications/mod.rs:143,151; enterprise_application.rs:74,77; managed_identity.rs:57,60; permissions.rs:55,58 (`tracing::debug!(target = "azapptoolkit::cache", kind = "Lists", key = %key, "hit")`).
tracing-0.1 macros.rs:21,55,663: the target override is spelled `target: $target:expr`; `$($k:ident).+ = $($fields:tt)*` is the field arm.
lib.rs:359-365:
  .with(fmt::layer().with_target(false).compact())
  .with(fmt::layer().with_ansi(false).with_target(false).with_writer(file_writer))
rationale: The authors intended a stable logical target so operators could filter `azapptoolkit::cache=debug`; instead each line gains a bogus `target="azapptoolkit::cache"` field, the real target stays the module path, and the intended filter matches nothing. Because both fmt layers set `with_target(false)`, the support file shows no module attribution at all — a `warn` from the graph crate, the auth crate or a command is indistinguishable except by message text (the README's `azapptoolkit_graph=trace` advice works only because the real target is the module path).
proposal: Replace `target = "..."` with `target: "..."` at the 13 sites (compile-checked), and turn `with_target(true)` on for the FILE layer only (keep stdout compact). Add a repo-invariant test that greps for `tracing::\w+!\(\s*target =` to keep the misspelling from returning. Effort S.
verifier_notes: Verified against tracing 0.1.44 (Cargo.lock) macros.rs: the `debug!`/`warn!` arms spell the target override `target: $target:expr` (arms at lines 88-100 of the macro), and `target = "..."` falls into the field arm `($($k:ident).+ = $($field:tt)*)` (line 181), so it is recorded as a field named `target` while the real target stays module_path!(). The repo itself demonstrates the correct form — the auth crate and state.rs use `target: "auth"` (crates/azapptoolkit-auth/src/service/mod.rs:175,192; token_cache.rs:366; state.rs:351,366; commands/auth.rs:41) — so the intent is clear and the 12 misspelled sites (not 13: service_principals.rs:189,209,216,257; applications/mod.rs:143,151; enterprise_application.rs:74,77; managed_identity.rs:57,60; permissions.rs:55,58) are a slip. Both fmt layers set `.with_target(false)` (lib.rs:359-365), so the file carries no module attribution either. No repo_invariants test guards tracing macro syntax (files: cache, cancel, commands, fanout, release, sources, trust). Proposal (fix spelling, `with_target(true)` on the file layer only, grep-based invariant) fits repo conventions. Low is honest.

title: DEVELOPMENT.md says the NSIS installer 'asks once about per-user vs per-machine'; the config uses Tauri's default currentUser mode, so nothing asks
rationale: Tauri's NSIS `installMode` defaults to `currentUser`; only `both` shows the per-user/per-machine chooser. `bundle.windows` sets nothing for NSIS, so the installer silently installs per-user — which is also what the README and the release-body row ("per-user, auto-updates") say and what the updater's passive `/P /UPDATE` relaunch relies on (a per-machine NSIS install would need elevation the passive updater does not request). DEVELOPMENT.md therefore contradicts both the shipped behaviour and the sibling docs; a contributor who 'fixes' the config to `both` to match the doc would break silent updates for anyone who picked per-machine.
proposal: Rewrite the sentence to "installs per-user with no prompt and no admin rights (Tauri's default `currentUser` NSIS mode — keep it that way: the passive updater relaunch depends on it)". One-line docs edit; optionally pin with a repo_invariants check that `bundle.windows.nsis.installMode` is absent or `currentUser`.
verifier_notes: Docs contradiction confirmed. docs/DEVELOPMENT.md:179-181 says the NSIS installer 'asks once about per-user vs per-machine'; apps/desktop/src-tauri/tauri.conf.json:38-42 sets only `webviewInstallMode` (no `nsis.installMode`) and updater-build.json only `createUpdaterArtifacts`; vendored tauri-utils-2.9.3/src/config.rs:822-841 marks `NSISInstallerMode::CurrentUser` as `#[default]`, and Tauri's installer.nsi (tauri-cli-v2.11.5, :113-126, :179-181) inserts the `MULTIUSER_PAGE_INSTALLMODE` chooser only for `both`. README.md:189-190 and release.yml:295 both already say per-user, so DEVELOPMENT.md is the odd one out. One nuance in the rationale: with `both` the template sets `MULTIUSER_EXECUTIONLEVEL Highest` (and the config doc at :835-837 notes `both` requires admin even for a per-user install), so a per-machine update would raise a UAC prompt from the installer rather than fail outright — the passive `/P /UPDATE` relaunch would stop being prompt-free, not break. Suggested wording therefore: 'installs per-user with no prompt and no admin rights (Tauri's default currentUser NSIS mode — keep it: it is what README/release body promise and it keeps the passive update UAC-free)'. The optional repo_invariants pin fits the existing tauri.conf.json assertions in repo_invariants/release.rs. Severity low is honest.

evidence:

    CEILING_MB=52
    DEPS=target/wasm32-unknown-unknown/debug/deps` (measures `gui_*.wasm` test shards only)

Do not add it to `verify-full` (which builds the frontend in debug and mirrors CI's debug-only `web` job); instead document `just web-build-release && just web-size` as the local way to check, and record the current baseline numbers in docs/architecture/release-updater-demo.md next to the crypto pins.

The measurement belongs where release builds already happen.
